brief: I'm a backend engineer at Marlowe Ferries and I need a one-page orientation for the three developers who join on Monday 2026-10-12; they will open it from a link in the team chat, on laptops. Show how a ticket purchase travels through our booking service as two paths the reader can tell apart at a glance. The path the customer waits on: Browser, Edge proxy (4 ms), Booking service (22 ms), Seat store (35 ms), Payment provider (410 ms), then back to the Browser, all inside a 600 ms budget; the payment call is the only step that has ever blown it. The path the customer does not wait on: once payment succeeds, the Booking service puts a message on the Receipts queue, the Receipt worker (about 2 s) writes to the Ledger and passes it to the Mailer, which sends the confirmation within 90 s. Draw the waiting path in ferry blue (#1F5FA8) and the background path in amber (#D98A1B), and mark every step that can fail without the customer noticing. Title it 'How a ticket gets booked'. When the link is pasted into chat, the preview line should read: Where a Marlowe ticket purchase waits, and where it doesn't.

Our steering group meets Thursday 2026-10-22 to decide whether to fund a second validation worker, and I, the data operations lead at Kestrel Grain Co-op, will project this page in the room, so it has to read from the back row. Draw the daily silo-readings pipeline left to right. Normal path: 1,840 Silo sensors send readings every 5 minutes to the Collector (1 minute), which writes to the Raw landing area; Validation (3 minutes) checks each batch, about 11,500 a day, and passes good ones to the Clean store; the Nightly rollup (40 minutes, starts 01:30) feeds the Yield dashboard that agronomists open at 07:00. Failure path: when Validation rejects a batch, which happened to 2.3% of batches in September, it goes to Quarantine, pages the on-call analyst, and waits for manual review (target 4 hours); once fixed, the batch is replayed into Validation. Show the failure path in brick red (#B3261E) and also with dashed lines, so it still stands out when someone prints it in black and white. Mark the point where the dashboard goes stale: any batch still in Quarantine at 06:00. Close with the decision line: fund the second worker at £3,400 a month, or keep reviewing by hand.

Halvorsen Mutual's network review is Friday 2026-11-13, and the team leads will have this open on their laptops during the call while we go through who owns what. Draw the network as it stands: a central Transit hub in the Shared-Network account (10.10.0.0/16) connecting Claims-Prod (10.20.0.0/16), Billing-Prod (10.30.0.0/16), Audit (10.90.0.0/16) and Sandbox (10.99.0.0/16), plus the Datacentre link (172.16.0.0/12), which arrives over two redundant tunnels, Tunnel A and Tunnel B. All outbound internet traffic passes one Firewall in Shared-Network, and Audit receives a copy of the flow logs from every other account. The point of the page is ownership: let the reader pick a team and see everything that team owns lit up while the rest fades back. Platform owns the Transit hub and both tunnels (teal, #1B7F79); Security owns Audit and the Firewall (plum, #7B3F7F); Claims owns Claims-Prod (orange, #C8641B); Billing owns Billing-Prod (navy, #24407A). Sandbox has no owner; show it in grey (#8A8F98) so it stands out as a question to settle. With no team picked, show every item in its owner's colour. Title: 'Who owns the network'.

The assessor arrives on 2026-11-30 and has asked us for a printed picture of how a card payment moves through our systems, with the payment card boundary clearly drawn. I'm the compliance manager at Quillon Books, and the sheet will be read on paper in black and white, so don't rely on colour alone. The flow: Shopper, Checkout page (the card fields come from Paysmith, our hosted form provider), Payment connector, Paysmith gateway, Acquirer (Northgate Acquiring), Card network, Issuing bank, and the answer returns the same way. The connector swaps the card number for a token and keeps only the token in the Token vault; the Order service, Receipt mailer, Warehouse system, Refund desk and Loyalty points only ever see that token. Fraud scoring gets the order total and postcode, never the card number. Of our 14 systems, 5 are inside the boundary: Checkout page, Payment connector, Token vault, Masked log store and Paysmith gateway; the other 9 are the five token-only systems, Fraud scoring, and the three outside parties. Give me the full flow as the main picture, and a second view of the same drawing that outlines the boundary, labels the 5 in-scope systems, and fades the other 9. We take about 38,000 card payments a month.

Make me a page for my phone that shows why our builds take 42 minutes when the goal is 30. I'm the engineering manager at Fernhill Games, I check it between meetings holding the phone upright, and I forward it to the leads afterwards. The stages in order, with minutes: Commit, then Lint (1) and Unit tests (4) side by side, then Build (6), Integration tests (22), Package (3), Deploy to staging (5) and Smoke tests (2). A Security scan (9) runs alongside Integration tests and never holds anything up. Show the slow path, the chain of stages that sets the 42 minutes, in tomato red (#D6452F), and the stages that wait for nobody in quiet grey; put each stage's minutes on it and the running total at the end of each step on the slow path. Tell me in one line which single stage is the problem. Then show the same pipeline again with Integration tests split into 4 equal parts of about 6 minutes, and the new total of 26, so I can see the gain at a glance. Add a note that the nightly Full device matrix (3 h 10 min) is separate and stays as it is.

Next Wednesday, 2026-10-28, I'll share my screen on a video call and need a page I can step through live to explain how orders flow at Petalbridge Florals. Five services (Orders, Payments, Inventory, Fulfilment, Notifications) talk only by publishing and listening to events on one shared bus; none calls another directly. Events: OrderPlaced (published by Orders; heard by Payments and Inventory), PaymentCaptured (Payments; heard by Orders and Fulfilment), StockReserved (Inventory; heard by Fulfilment), OrderPacked (Fulfilment; heard by Notifications and Orders), OrderShipped (Fulfilment; heard by Notifications and Orders). Failure case: if Inventory cannot hold the stems it publishes StockUnavailable, which Payments hears and answers with PaymentRefunded, heard by Orders and Notifications. Draw the whole system once, then give me five steps to advance one at a time (placed, paid, reserved, packed, shipped) plus a sixth that shows the stock failure in place of the last three. Each step lights up only the events and services in play and says in one line what just happened. Mention that 6,200 orders arrived on Valentine's Eve, 2026-02-13, which is why we decoupled. The audience includes finance and will watch the shared screen, so use plain labels.

The finance subcommittee of the Anselm County Libraries board votes on 2026-11-12 on moving our catalogue off our own servers, and as IT lead I need one page they can open from an emailed link on their laptops. Draw the system once and let the reader switch between Before and After, with everything that stays in place staying put. Before: 17 Branch terminals connect to the Catalogue server in the Harlow office (two machines, one hot spare), which reads the Patron database on the same machines; a Tape backup runs nightly at 23:00; loans between branches are reconciled by hand each morning at the central desk. After: the same Branch terminals connect to a Hosted catalogue; patron records sit in a Managed database in the provider's region, with continuous backup replacing the tape; a Loan exchange does the reconciling automatically. Mark each item as kept, replaced, new or retired, and show the yearly running cost under the drawing in both states: £61,000 before, £44,500 after. Cut-over is the weekend of 2026-11-21, with up to 9 hours when the catalogue is read-only. The risk they have asked about: if cut-over fails we return to the old servers, which stay powered until 2026-12-19.

Engineers on call at Cinderwick Audio, a podcast hosting company, keep asking where a missing log line or a flat graph went, and they will read the answer on their phones at 3 a.m., so keep it narrow and easy to scan. Draw two separate paths, one above the other, starting from the same services. Logs (violet, #6B4FBB): the Player, Upload and Billing services write to standard output; the Log agent on each host forwards every 12 seconds to the Log shipper, which batches to the Search cluster; a line is searchable about 20 seconds after it is written, kept 14 days, then moved to the Cold archive for 13 months. Metrics (lime green, #6AA121): each service exposes counters; the Collector reads them every 15 seconds into the Metrics store (kept 90 days); Alert rules are checked every 60 seconds and send a page after 2 failures in a row; Dashboards read the Metrics store. Mark the three places where data can be lost: the Log agent buffer (256 MB, drops oldest when full), the Shipper queue (holds 10 minutes), and the Collector's 10-second read timeout. Next to each, one line saying what to check first. Show the delay at each step. Title it 'Where did my data go?'

Draft a one-page handout for Thursday's lunch-and-learn for the new developers at Dunmore Tea Merchants; I'll print it on A4 and hand it out, so it must stay readable on paper. The topic is how our product catalogue lookups use a cache that sits beside the database. Reads: the app asks the Cache first; on a hit it answers in about 2 ms; on a miss it asks the Database (about 45 ms), puts the answer in the Cache with a 10-minute lifetime, and then answers. Writes: the app updates the Database first, then deletes that product's entry from the Cache, so the next read refills it. Draw these as two numbered flows, Read and Write, on one sheet. Add a worked example: 'Lapsang Souchong 250 g' changes from £8.40 to £8.90 at 14:05, and show what a shopper sees before and after the change. Add the numbers that justify it: at the 4,000 reads per second we see at peak and a 92% hit rate, the database serves 320 a second instead of 4,000. Finish with one boxed warning about the race where a slow read that started before a write puts the old price back into the Cache, and say it can last up to 10 minutes.

We need a wall poster for the operations room at Transportes Ordóñez, printed large and read from a few metres away, so keep labels big and few. Write it all in Spanish, keeping the service names as written: the main title must read 'El camino de una petición' and the heading of the second picture 'Vista de la entrada'. Main picture: a request from a customer's browser goes through the Load balancer, then the Ingress controller (2 copies), then the right Service, then one of its Pods, then out to the Database outside the cluster, and the answer returns the same way. Our 9 Pods run on 3 nodes and belong to three services: tracking-web (3), tracking-api (4) and quotes (2). Second picture, the same layout, zooms in on the entrance and lists the routing rules: seguimiento.ordonez-transportes.example with the path / goes to tracking-web; the same host with the path /api goes to tracking-api; cotizaciones.ordonez-transportes.example goes to quotes. Show on it that encryption ends at the Ingress controller, that a request waits at most 30 seconds, and that each caller is capped at 200 requests per second. Use deep green (#1E6B4A) for the path through the cluster and signal orange (#E8741E) for the entrance.

Please turn last month's outage into a page for the executives, who will read it on tablets at Monday's briefing. I'm the head of reliability at Tarnwick Bookings; the outage was 2026-10-03. Timeline: 09:12 a configuration change went to the Session service; 09:19 its error rate reached 18%; 09:24 the first alert fired; 09:31 we declared the incident; 09:48 rollback started; 10:05 everything recovered. Show this as a flow from cause to effect: the change, Session service errors, Login failures, then the pages that depend on login, with the clock times on the way. Then show the blast radius on the same flow: Login failed for 100% of attempts, Checkout for 61%, Booking changes were degraded, Search and Admin untouched. Colour what was hit in crimson (#C0283C), degraded in gold (#D9A520), and untouched in pale grey. Put the headline numbers at the top: 53 minutes of impact, 41,300 sessions affected, 1,120 support tickets, an estimated €212,000 in lost bookings. Detection took 12 minutes; finish with the one change we are making: alert at a 2% error rate instead of 15%, to detect within 5 minutes.

Partner developers keep asking us what happens to their request between the moment it reaches Wrenfield Payroll and the moment it hits a backend, so I want a reference page they can open from a link on a laptop while they build against us. Show the path: Client, Gateway edge, Auth check, Rate limiter, Router, then one of three backends (Employees, Timesheets, Payslips), and the response back out. Give me the one full picture, plus two more views of the same drawing that the reader can switch between. Auth view: highlight where a key is exchanged for a token at the Auth check (tokens last 15 minutes), where scopes are checked (employees:read, timesheets:write, payslips:read), and the two ways to fail: 401 when the token is missing or expired, 403 when the scope is wrong. Rate limit view: highlight the Rate limiter and show Standard keys at 100 requests per minute, Premium at 600, a burst allowance of 20, and what a caller gets when over the limit: 429 with a Retry-After header counting down in seconds. Use slate blue (#3B5B92) for auth and rust (#B5532A) for rate limits. The one-sentence description when the link is shared: How a Wrenfield API call is checked and limited before it reaches us.
